This procedural subject-matter conclusion does not establish the existence, validity, duration or continued operation of the plaintiffs' asserted tenancy.

requests.text: The presence of a special-Act trust-inquiry prayer alongside a civil-adjudicable tenancy controversy does not alone justify rejection of the whole plaint under Order VII Rule 11(a) or (d). This does not foreclose another properly established whole-plaint ground for rejection or prove that any requested remedy must be granted.

requests.text: The procedural availability of civil adjudication concerning tenancy does not establish forcible dispossession, a right to restoration under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, or entitlement to an injunction. The disputed possession event and the separate discretionary injunction questions remain matters for relevant evidence and appropriate merits assessment. This is an analytically supported distinction, not a completed mechanical evaluation or a substantive merits ruling.

counterarguments: The trust contended under Order VII Rule 11(a) and (d) that the plaint lacked a real cause of action and that Sections 50, 51 and 80 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act barred ordinary civil adjudication; lower courts accepted rejection (IK-1841885:L69-L76, L80-L82).

Rule 11 also authorizes rejecting a genuinely illusory, manifestly vexatious or legally barred whole plaint; omitted necessary material facts cannot be supplied by particulars (IK-1841885:L103-L105, L119-L126).

Order VII Rule 11 does not allow rejection of only a part of a plaint; Order VI Rule 16 is a different procedure, and giving up reliefs requires appropriate trial-court application subject to Order II consequences (IK-1841885:L105, L117-L118, L131-L132, L137).

The court agreed that prayer D for investigation into trust affairs belongs to Section 50 and, for suits within its class, the Section 51 prior-consent regime; this objection cannot automatically displace the distinct tenancy subject (IK-1841885:L133-L136).

The trust denied forcible eviction, asserted possession was lawfully taken, and invoked voluntary surrender by 22 of 44 tenants; the identities of surrendering tenants, disposal timing and relevance of the interim injunction remain unproved (IK-1841885:L138, L151-L152).

Section 6 permits certain claims by dispossessed settled possessors even without title, whereas equitable injunction against a true owner is subject to different discretionary restrictions; no findings established the plaintiffs' facts under either standard (IK-1841885:L139-L150).

The trust raised arrears, alleged failures to comply with previous writ interim directions, and a District-Court-only jurisdiction objection; their relevance was reserved and the last specific objection was expressly not decided (IK-1841885:L74-L82, L152-L153).

all_raw_relations.reason: The recorded invocation of Rule 11(a) and (d) supplies the procedural setting in which the whole-plaint screening framework operates.
The identified plaint supplies the pleading whose material averments and requested reliefs must be evaluated together.
The trial court accepted objections corresponding to the trust's asserted lack of cause of action and statutory-jurisdiction position; the appellate courts affirmed the rejection.
The lower-court treatment of the trust-law jurisdiction objection conflicts with the Supreme Court's distinction preserving civil adjudication of the tenancy subject.
The lower courts' whole-plaint rejection conflicts with the target court's reasoning that mixed prayers do not automatically defeat the separate tenancy cause.
The alleged continuing tenancy is a pleaded factual subject supporting the court's identification of the main controversy; the support does not establish tenancy validity.
The plaintiffs' 11-year position demonstrates that tenancy duration was substantively contested without proving the proposed term.
The trust's competing 11-month position supports identification of a real duration dispute, not the factual accuracy of the shorter term.
The parties assert incompatible durations for the disputed tenancy transaction; neither claimed duration was determined by the Supreme Court.

The requested tenancy declaration is consistent with the court's characterization of the tenancy relationship as the principal pleaded subject, although the prayer alone does not prove a cause of action.
Meaningful consideration of the whole plaint supplies the method used to identify the substantive tenancy controversy rather than mechanically classifying the suit by isolated prayers.
The Supreme Court's finding that the principal dispute concerns tenancy continuation and duration supplies the case-specific subject characterization underlying its civil-adjudicability reasoning.
The distinct prayer directing an inquiry into allegedly illegal trust acts supplies the case-specific request to which the Section 50 trust-affairs route applies.
The inquiry prayer coexists with the tenancy prayers, but its inclusion does not determine the legal or factual validity of the tenancy dispute; the court treated the subjects as distinct.
The whole-plaint approach and distinction between material facts and prayers undermine automatic rejection based solely on combining different requested reliefs.
The existence of an identified civil-adjudicable tenancy subject is a necessary part of explaining why the distinct special-Act prayer did not by itself defeat the entire plaint.
The separately classified trust-affairs inquiry shows why the special-Act issue can be distinguished from the civil tenancy subject rather than extended automatically to all requested reliefs.
The trust's argument that statutory restrictions justified rejection of the entire plaint is the competing position rejected by the Supreme Court's mixed-relief analysis.

The nonautomatic-rejection reasoning contributes to the Supreme Court's procedural restriction of continued adjudication to the tenancy subject. The direction of support runs from reasoning to disposition, not from disposition to its own justification.
Civil adjudicability of the tenancy subject explains the particular subject-matter scope of the court's procedural direction.

The distinct statutory treatment of the trust inquiry helps explain why the court contemplated lawful applications to give up other reliefs, without proving that an application was actually submitted.
The plaintiffs' allegation supplies the affirmative asserted version of unlawful dispossession, but it does not establish the allegation as a proved fact.
The trust's denial and assertion of lawful taking directly contest the plaintiffs' characterization of the same possession event.
The recorded plaintiffs' allegation supplies one of the two party assertions underlying the procedural record of opposed dispossession accounts.
The trust's recorded denial and lawful-taking assertion supply the opposing account, without being adopted as true.

Trust counsel invoked surrender by 22 tenants as context for lawful possession-taking, but the judgment does not identify those tenants as the plaintiffs or establish that their transactions explain the disputed taking.
An asserted numerical pattern of voluntary surrenders does not resolve whether the identified plaintiffs themselves consented or were lawfully dispossessed.
The injunction's period of operation may affect the possession controversy, but the judgment lacks the dates needed to determine its effect.
The recorded opposition of the parties' accounts provides the procedural context for the Supreme Court's express refusal to decide the disputed forcible-possession merits.
The Section 6 standard requires assessment of actual possession circumstances; the plaintiffs' settled-possession status is not established.
The conflicting dispossession accounts do not establish the nonconsensual and unlawful dispossession facts needed for plaintiff-specific Section 6 recovery.
Potential restoration under Section 6 and equitable injunction entitlement follow different analyses; the restoration standard does not establish an injunction right.
The general injunction restriction requires plaintiff-specific findings about possession and other equitable factors that were not supplied in this review.
The court expressly left disputed possession issues open, and its discussion of injunction standards did not decide the separate question of equitable entitlement.

The procedural distinction between a sustainable tenancy subject and the grant of requested remedies is consistent with expressly leaving the disputed possession allegations for possible relevant consideration at trial.
